extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, memoirists, and creative-writing workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative point(s) of view (POV) — involved/omniscient, detached/objective, limited third, observer-narrator, first person, unreliable narration — and on when/how to shift POV. Includes exercises to practise these voices and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involved Author (authorial narration / omniscient author)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who 'knows what’s going on in all the different places the characters are at the same time, and what’s going on inside the characters, and what has happened, and what has to happen.' (Le Guin prefers 'involved author' to the pejorative 'omniscient author.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versatile, flexible, and complex but difficult to handle; openly manipulative of POV. Can move between characters’ minds and the author's voice; can drop into many voices (even animals) and back. Use when you are profoundly involved with the material and have a reason to address the reader directly. Examples: Tolstoy, Dickens, Tolkien (fox glimpse), Woolf (voice of the book). Quick unsignaled shifting in this voice is rare and requires immense skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached Author (fly-on-the-wall / camera eye / objective narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who is not one of the characters and reports only what a neutral observer could infer from behavior and speech; the author never enters a character’s mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values and judgments can only be implied indirectly. This cool, restrained voice is good practice for writers who otherwise rely on readers to mirror their emotional responses; mastering it can produce very moving work. Popular around 1900 and in 'minimalist' fiction (e.g., Raymond Carver). Use when you want implied judgments and emotional reserve. Example: the Princess Sefrid detached-author excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited Third Person
rubrics_metrics.description: A third-person narration limited to the perceptions, thoughts, and voice of a single viewpoint character (the predominant modern fictional voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because perception is limited, you must not present what the viewpoint character cannot know. Shifts within limited third (from one character’s mind to another’s) require equal awareness and care — they must be signalled and justified. One-word or momentary shifts out of the viewpoint (e.g., describing what the viewpoint character’s eyes look like to others) are uncomfortable and betray POV rules unless explicitly framed as the character’s thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer-Narrator (first-person witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator is one of the characters but not the principal actor; the story is about events the narrator witnessed and wants to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in both fiction and nonfiction; because the observer-narrator is not the protagonist, readers can usually assume this narrator is fairly reliable or at least transparent. Use to give an eyewitness perspective without centering the narrator’s life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer-Narrator (third-person)
rubrics_metrics.description: A viewpoint limited to an observer character but told in third person (limited third used for an observer-narrator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distances the whole story; unreliability is less of an issue because the narrator is an onlooker, though the narrator’s limited knowledge shapes the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-Person Narration and Memoir Constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person is the voice most memoirists use, but memoirists do not have the right to be omniscient about other real people's thoughts and motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoirists must not present others’ unverified thoughts as facts; if you speculate about another’s motives you must clearly indicate that it is your interpretation or guess. To practise other POVs, memoirists should invent characters and write fictionally rather than trespass on real people’s inner lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose account cannot be taken at face value; unreliability is a complex and subtle way of showing narrator character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read for omissions and inconsistencies; the reader must look through what the narrator says to what is left out. Example: Henry James’ 'The Turn of the Screw.' Use unreliability deliberately as a device rather than accidentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing Point of View — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting POV is possible but risky: any shift from one of the defined POVs to another is a major change of voice that will affect tone and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware, have a reason, and be in control of all shifts of viewpoint character. Inconsistent or frequent, unsignalled POV changes jerk the reader around, confuse emotion, and garble the story. Know when and how to shift so the reader is carried effortlessly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting between first and third person
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving from first to third person (or vice versa) within a piece is enormously difficult and uncommon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do it only with a really good reason and with great care (Bleak House’s alternation is a special, artificial device and creates jolts). Avoid in short pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting between detached and involved authorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching between a detached 'fly-on-the-wall' voice and a fully involved authorial voice within the same piece is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two modes are fundamentally different in manipulation and presence; you really can’t (or shouldn’t) shift between them inside one piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifts within limited third person (between characters’ minds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting from one character’s consciousness to another’s while using limited third-person viewpoint is possible but demands equal awareness and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal such shifts clearly (line breaks, paragraphing, labels) and have a reason; avoid very frequent shifts or shifts that last only a moment. Frequent uncontrolled shifts tire readers and cause confusion about whose mind we're in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid one-word or momentary POV intrusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, unmarked intrusions that attribute knowledge the viewpoint character cannot have (one-word POV shifts) are uncomfortable and incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you wish to present something from another character’s perception, either shift viewpoint properly or make it explicit that the viewpoint character is thinking about it (e.g., 'She raised her eyes, knowing the effect...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Signalling POV changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When you do change viewpoint, mark it clearly so the reader is carried with you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible signals include paragraph indents, line breaks, naming the narrator in parentheses at section heads, or other devices; Woolf uses paragraphing and perceptual cues to make transitions effortless and clear. Marking shifts prevents jolts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling unspoken thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters’ unspoken thoughts must be presented clearly as interior events and are handled like dialogue if presented directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: tag thoughts as thought ('Aunt Jane thought...'), use indirect interior speech ('As soon as she heard... she knew...'), or free indirect style. You don’t have to use quotation marks; typographical devices (italics) can overemphasize and editors may convert thoughts to italics. Make it clear the material is inside someone’s head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of POV affects tone, effect, and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of point(s) of view and the voice in which a story is told can make an immense difference to tone, effect, and even meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story may 'stick' until you find the right person to tell it; experiment with first vs third, involved author vs limited third, participant vs bystander, or multiple narrators to find the effect you want. The book gives reading recommendations (Atwood, Hillerman, Paretsky, etc.) to study genre-specific POV uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises to practice POV (Exercise Seven and Eight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured exercises to build POV awareness: write a 200–350-word sketch involving several people with little/no dialogue; Part One: two versions in limited third from two participants; Part Two: retell with detached narrator; Part Three: add an observer-narrator; Part Four: write in involved-author POV (may expand to ~1000 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise Eight extends this: Quick Shifts in Limited Third (300–600 words) — change viewpoint characters with clear markers; Thin Ice (300–1000 words) — deliberately shift POV several times without obvious signals to practise the technique (likely to become involved-author). Use the exercises to become superconscious of POV choices and shifts. Optional additions: tell the story twice in first person, try voices you dislike, compare detached vs viewpoint versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try voices you dislike and recombine exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: If there’s a mode or voice you don’t like, that’s probably the one you should try again to discover why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-run the exercises with different stories or recombine instruction parts. Trying disliked modes can reveal their strengths and increase your flexibility as a writer.
